agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: That ranking is not informative. A standardized difference between two groups with a 26% minority is capped near 2.3, and dozens of neurons in every layer sit at that cap. Practically every unit shifts once an answer becomes a loop, so answer averages can't single out a responsible component. I need token-level data. I'll teacher-force the model's own looping answers, plus a few long finished answers as controls, and record MLP activations at 13 layers (every odd layer) together with token logprobs. Then within each text I can compare tokens that continue an already-seen n-gram (copying) with tokens that don't. This is the repeated-vs-novel contrast used to find "repetition neurons", and it removes the problem-difficulty confound. If a small set of neurons is strongly and specifically more active on repeated tokens, those are candidates to ablate. If the contrast is again diffuse, I'll turn to attention.

The 32 texts total about 25k tokens, padded to 965 each, which comes to about 5.5 GB for 13 MLP layers, within the 6 GB limit. I'll run the teacher-forced pass on the original model, collecting MLP activations at odd layers and per-token logprobs. In the kernel I'll then mark copied tokens (the preceding 8-gram occurred earlier in the answer) and compare neuron activations on copied vs novel answer tokens.

The teacher-forced pass returned MLP activations for the 32 texts, 24 looping and 8 finished. I'll label every answer token as copied (the 8-gram ending at it already occurred earlier in the answer) or novel. Per neuron and layer, I'll compute the effect size of copied minus novel tokens, using only within-answer tokens from the looping texts. As a sanity check, I'll also confirm that copied tokens get near-certain logprobs, as expected in a greedy loop. A small set of neurons with large, consistent effect sizes, unlike the diffuse answer-mean picture, would be repetition-neuron candidates. If the top effect sizes are only moderate and spread everywhere, this line is weak.

The token-level contrast is clearer than the answer-mean one. Copied tokens are near-deterministic (mean logprob -0.013 vs -0.117 for novel tokens), and a few neurons, concentrated in layers 9-15, separate copied from novel tokens with effect sizes of 1.0-1.3. The 99th percentile of the effect size is only 0.5-0.7, so these are clear outliers. The top ones (L13 n486, n1926, n4180; L9 n5659; L15 n386, n5730) are the same units that topped the answer-mean comparison, which is a consistency check. One confound remains: copied tokens sit later in the text than novel ones. So I'll check the position dependence of these neurons on the 8 finished controls, which have no loops, early vs late tokens. I'll also count how many neurons pass an effect-size threshold, to size an ablation set. If the top neurons are flat with position in the controls, they track repetition itself and are worth an ablation test.
